title: Gini index & entropy: measuring impurity
intro: The measure behind every split, up close: what Gini and entropy really mean (a probability, a number of bits), how to compute them and why the choice almost never matters.
keyPoints: Impurity compresses “how mixed is this node” into one number: 0 = every sample the same class, maximal = a perfectly uniform mix. Gini and entropy are the two standard measures.
Gini = 1 − Σ pk² — literally the probability that two random samples from the node have different classes; ceiling 1 − 1/K.
Entropy = −Σ pk log₂ pk — the uncertainty about the class of a random sample, in bits; ceiling log₂ K.
The best split has the highest information gain: parent impurity minus the weighted child impurity — the number the greedy tree maximises.
The measures are strongly correlated (Gini ≤ H/2, equal at 50/50): they pick virtually the same splits. Gini is the fast default, entropy the ID3/C4.5 classic in bits.

blocks.html: Every splitting strategy needs one impurity measure: a function giving each group a single score — 0 for perfectly pure, higher for more mixed.
Every usable measure shares three properties: zero for a pure node, maximal for a uniform mix and symmetric in the classes (80% ✓ is as impure as 20% ✓).
The two measures dominating practice: the Gini index (scikit-learn default, from CART) and entropy (from Shannon's information theory, used by ID3/C4.5).

sections.title: The Gini index: the odds of two draws

blocks.html: Gini is the most literal measure: draw two random samples from the node (with replacement) — the chance they have a different class is exactly the node's Gini. Pure node: 0; 50/50 mix: 0.5.

blocks.label: Gini impurity
blocks.caption: pk is the fraction of samples of class k in the node; K is the number of classes. For two classes the formula reduces to 2p(1−p): the parabola from the plot in Decision trees.

blocks.html: Three classes (50% buy, 30% hold, 20% sell): \( G = 1 - (0.5^2 + 0.3^2 + 0.2^2) = 0.62 \). Ceiling for a uniform mix over K classes: \( 1 - \tfrac{1}{K} \) (2 classes: 0.5; 3: 0.667).
Arithmetically Gini is the cheap one: only squares, no logarithms — and a tree evaluates thousands of candidate splits. That is why Gini is the CART and scikit-learn default.

Name confusion: the Gini index from economics (income inequality) is a distant cousin. In ML contexts “Gini” almost always means the impurity version — and the measure says nothing about which class wins.

Entropy measures uncertainty in bits: the minimum average number of yes/no questions the smartest possible strategy needs to classify a drawn sample. Pure node: 0 questions; 50/50 mix: exactly 1 question (1 bit).

blocks.label: Entropy
blocks.caption: In bits, because the base is 2. Convention: 0·log 0 = 0 — an absent class contributes nothing. Maximum log<sub>2</sub> K at a uniform mix: 1 bit for two classes, 1.585 for three.

blocks.html: Same sentiment node: \( H = -(0.5 \log_2 0.5 + 0.3 \log_2 0.3 + 0.2 \log_2 0.2) = 1.485 \) bits. The question game averages 1.5 questions — entropy 1.485 is the sharp lower bound.

The scales differ (H = 1.485 vs G = 0.62), but the tree always compares splits within the same measure — only the ordering matters. Real difference: Gini's ceiling is \( 1 - 1/K < 1 \), entropy grows without bound as \( \log_2 K \).
Three rules: \( -\log_2 p \) is positive for p < 1; every halving of p costs one extra bit; base 2 gives bits, the natural logarithm nats (1 bit ≈ 0.693 nats).

sections.title: The two measures side by side: Gini ≈ H/2

blocks.html: Plot both measures against the mix ratio and the curves nearly coincide: the entropy curve has exactly the bell shape of the Gini parabola, roughly twice as tall. Structurally: \( G \le H/2 \) for every distribution, with equality at p = 0.5.
At p = 0.5 Gini and H/2 coincide exactly (both 0.5); elsewhere the difference is at most ~0.05 — and since the tree only compares orderings, that is meaningless.

blocks.title: The (entropy, Gini) plane
blocks.subtitle: Every dot is one class distribution: entropy horizontally, Gini vertically. The magenta dots are binary nodes (p = 0.1 … 0.5); your green dot follows the three class counters A/B/C. Set one counter to 0 and you drop exactly onto the binary arc; make them equal (e.g. 4/4/4) and you slide to the uniform maximum — still just below the line. Keep at least one counter above zero.

metrics.label: Gini − H/2
metrics.expr: 1 - (a*a + b*b + c*c) / ((a+b+c)*(a+b+c)) - ((a+b+c) <= 0 ? NaN : Math.log2((a+b+c)) - ((a>1e-9? a*Math.log2(a):0) + (b>1e-9? b*Math.log2(b):0) + (c>1e-9? c*Math.log2(c):0)) / (a+b+c)) / 2

blocks.html: In the plot: every dot is one class distribution. At (5, 3, 2) you sit at (1.485, 0.62); equal counters (4/4/4) slide to the uniform maximum (1.585, 0.667) — farther from the line than ever, still below it.

Why two measures? History: entropy (Shannon, 1948) entered trees first via ID3/C4.5; Gini came along in 1984 with Breiman's CART as a computationally cheaper alternative. You must be able to read both; you almost never have to choose.
The information gain is the drop in weighted average impurity — and since the parent is fixed within one split comparison, “highest gain” equals “lowest weighted child impurity”.

blocks.label: Information gain
blocks.caption: I is the chosen measure (Gini or entropy); n<sub>j</sub> is the number of samples in child j and n the total in the parent. The fraction weights each child by its size.

blocks.html: Node with 12 ✓ / 8 ✗ (p = 0.6), split into left 2✓/6✗ (p = 0.25) and right 10✓/2✗ (p = 0.833). Gini: parent 0.480, weighted children 0.317, gain 0.163. Entropy: 0.971 → 0.715, gain 0.256 bits.

Weighting with \( n_j/n \) is the heart of the measure: one small dirty leaf of 1/20 does not outweigh half-cleaning nineteen samples — however small a child, its impurity counts in proportion to its size.

Classic trap: a feature with many unique values (customer ID, timestamp) offers so many thresholds that a “perfect” split always fits in between — apparent high gain, actually memorization. C4.5 counters this with the gain ratio.

blocks.html: Practical advice: keep the default (Gini) and spend your tuning budget on max_depth, min_samples_leaf and min_samples_split. Pick entropy only if you need gains in bits.

blocks.html: Exactly the manual figures: Gini 0.480 → 0.317 (gain 0.163) and entropy 0.971 → 0.715 (gain 0.256 bits). Comparing the gains across measures is impossible — different scales — but the tree always chooses within its own scale.

blocks.caption: criterion="gini" versus "entropy" on breast_cancer
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

for criterion in ['gini', 'entropy']:
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion=criterion, random_state=42)
    tree.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f'criterion={criterion:8s} test-score={tree.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}  '
          f'leaves={tree.get_n_leaves()}')

blocks.html: Typical output: the Gini tree scores 0.951 with 16 leaves, the entropy tree 0.958 with 14. Related, not identical — but one point on one split is noise, not signal.
criterion is technically a hyperparameter — but one with a suspiciously small effect. The tree shape that does matter (depth, leaf size) is the subject of the bias-variance tradeoff.
